Yellowcake, also called urania, is a powdery form of uranium concentrate. It comes from solutions after processing uranium ores. Yellowcake is made after mining but before turning the uranium into fuel or enriching it further. The process to get yellowcake varies depending on the type of ore. First, the ore is ground and chemically treated. The result is a coarse powder that smells strong and doesn't dissolve in water. It contains about 80% uranium oxide, which melts at around 2880°C.

The Arc de Triomphe de l'Etoile is a famous monument in Paris, France. It's at the end of Champs-Élysées, in the center of Place Charles de Gaulle, which used to be called Place de l'Etoile—the "star" due to its twelve roads radiating from it. The monument stands between three parts of Paris: the 16th arrondissement (south and west), the 17th (north), and the 8th (east). It honors soldiers who fought for France in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, with their names on its surfaces. Beneath it lies a tomb for an unknown soldier from World War I. As part of Paris's "historic axis," a line of monuments and important streets leading to Grande Arche de la Défense, the Arc was designed by Jean Chalgrin in 1806. Sculptures on it show French youth against German warriors. Standing at about 50 meters tall and wide, with an inner vault nearly 30 meters high and 20 meters wide, it is a central landmark. In 1919, a pilot flew his plane through the arch as part of a victory parade after World War I ended. Before the Arc de Triomphe, Mexico City's Monumento a la Revolución was the tallest triumphal arch at about 65 meters high. Pyongyang’s Arch of Triumph is similar in design and slightly taller, while La Grande Arche near Paris is also very tall but not named an Arc de Triomphe.

Giuseppina Bozzacchi, born in Milan on November 23, 1853, was a young Italian dancer. At just 16 years old, she performed the role of Swanhilda in the ballet "Coppélia," created by Léo Delibes, for the Paris Opera Ballet. Bozzacchi had come to study dancing in Paris with Mme Dominique. Earlier, choreographer Arthur Saint-Léon and director Émile Perrin had been looking for someone to play Swanhilda but couldn't find a suitable dancer among those they considered, including Léontine Beaugrand and Angelina Fioretti. In 1868, the favorite ballerina of Saint-Léon was preparing for the role when she fell ill. In 1869, Saint-Léon and Perrin asked composer Léo Delibes to find a suitable Swanhilda on his trip to Italy. He didn't return with anyone but they found Bozzacchi, who performed the role of Swanhilda for the first time on May 25, 1870, in front of Emperor Napoleon III. Bozzacchi repeated her performance several times after that. However, in July, a war broke out between France and Prussia over Spain's throne. On July 19, France declared war. Bozzacchi danced Swanhilda for the last time on August 31, just before the Paris Opera closed due to the Franco-Prussian War. Due to the opera not paying salaries and a lack of food, Bozzacchi became weak and fell ill with smallpox and fever. She died in the morning of her 17th birthday and was buried at Cimetière de Montmartre in Paris.

On November 14, 2017, soldiers from the Zimbabwe Defence Forces (ZDF) surrounded Harare and took control of key areas. They also took over the Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation. The next day, ZDF said it was not a coup and President Robert Mugabe was safe but needed to deal with "criminals" around him who were causing problems. Tensions in Mugabe's ruling party, ZANU-PF, led to this event. Former first vice-president Emmerson Mnangagwa, supported by the ZDF, was fighting against first lady Grace Mugabe and her G40 faction over who would become the next leader after Mugabe turned 93. Before troops entered Harare, ZDF chief Constantino Chiwenga said purging senior officials like Mnangagwa had to stop. On November 19, ZANU-PF removed Mugabe as party leader and made Mnangagwa the new leader instead. They set a deadline for Mugabe to resign by November 20 or face removal from office. Mugabe did not resign, so on November 21, parliament held an impeachment session. Later that day, Mugabe sent a letter saying he was stepping down as president. Phelekezela Mphoko became acting president. Mnangagwa became the new president on November 24, 2017.

Cosmology is the study of the universe, from its beginning with the Big Bang and its development over time. It looks at how the universe started, how it has changed, and what might happen in the future. The Big Bang theory explains these things based on science. The term "cosmology" was first used in English in 1656 by Thomas Blount and later by Christian Wolff in 1731. It can include beliefs from religion or myths about how the universe began and what might happen at the end of time, but is mainly studied by scientists like astronomers and physicists. Philosophers, especially those who study space and time and metaphysics, also look into cosmology because it shares some areas with philosophy. However, theories in physical cosmology can include both scientific ideas that are testable and non-scientific ones that may not be. Cosmology focuses on the entire universe, unlike astronomy which looks at individual stars and planets. Modern cosmology is mostly based on the Big Bang theory combined with particle physics to explain how the universe works. The most common model today is called the Lambda-CDM model. Some scientists say cosmology is like a "historical science" because when we look at distant parts of space, we are seeing those places as they were in the past due to the time it takes for light to travel.

The Ontario New Democratic Party (NDP) is a social-democratic political party in Ontario, Canada. Since March 2009, Andrea Horwath has led this party, which currently forms the official opposition after the 2018 election. It is part of the federal New Democratic Party. Formed in October 1961 from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Ontario section) and the Ontario Federation of Labour (OFL), the NDP was most successful outside Canada's western heartland for many years. Donald C. MacDonald led it to its first big win in 1967, when they elected 20 members to the Ontario Legislative Assembly. In 1975, under Stephen Lewis' leadership, the party became official opposition for the first time since the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation did so twice in the 1940s. After poor performance in the 1977 election, which led to losing second place, Lewis resigned and Michael Cassidy took over as leader. However, he only led one campaign before resigning after a poor 1981 election result. Bob Rae became the new leader in 1982. In 1985, his party held power with the Liberals by signing an agreement. After the 1987 general election, they again formed official opposition. The 1990 election surprisingly resulted in the NDP winning its first government in Ontario's history, making it Canada's first New Democratic Party provincial government east of Manitoba. However, economic issues led to their defeat in 1995 and Rae stepped down. Howard Hampton was elected leader at a 1996 convention and led for three elections. He lost official party status after the 1999 and 2003 elections but regained it after winning several by-elections in the mid-2000s. The NDP kept its status after the 2007 election, and Hampton stepped down in 2009. Andrea Horwath replaced him as leader after winning at a Hamilton convention in 2009. Under her leadership, they won 17 seats in 2011 and 21 seats in 2014. In the 2018 election, under Horwath's guidance, they gained 40 seats to form official opposition again.

Very High Frequency (VHF) Omnidirectional Range (VOR) helps airplanes find their position and stay on course. Airplanes get information from fixed ground radio beacons using a receiver unit. VOR works with frequencies between 108.00 to 117.95 MHz in the VHF band. Developed starting in 1937, VOR became the standard air navigation system by 1946 and is used worldwide for both commercial and general aviation. By 2000, about 3,000 VOR stations were operating globally, with around 1,033 in the US; this number decreased to 967 by 2013 as GPS became more popular. A VOR ground station sends signals that rotate 30 times per second and a steady signal at 30 Hz. This helps airplanes find their direction from the beacon relative to magnetic north. Using signals from two different VOR stations, pilots can pinpoint their position. VOR coverage is limited to about 200 miles as it depends on line of sight between transmitter and receiver. Each station sends a VHF signal that includes navigation information, the station’s identifier in Morse code, and sometimes voice messages like station name, flight advisories, or live broadcasts.

A cave is a big space underground, large enough for a person to enter. Caves are often formed by weathering of rock and can go deep underground. However, strictly speaking, a cave must be deeper than it is wide, while a rock shelter has a wider opening. Speleology is the study of caves and their environments. Visiting or exploring caves for fun can be called caving, potholing, or spelunking.

Mikhail Bakunin (1814–1 July 1876) was a Russian revolutionary anarchist who founded collectivist anarchism. He is one of the most important figures in anarchism and helped start the social anarchist tradition. Bakunin was well-known as an activist, especially in Europe. Bakunin grew up on his family estate in Pryamukhino, Tver Governorate. From 1840, he studied in Moscow and then in Berlin to become a scholar. In Paris, he met Karl Marx and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, who greatly influenced him. His growing radical ideas made it impossible for him to have an academic job. He was expelled from France for opposing Russia's invasion of Poland. In 1849, Bakunin was arrested in Dresden during the Czech revolt of 1848 and deported to Russia. He spent time in prison and later exile in Siberia. Bakunin escaped through Japan to the United States and then London, where he worked on a journal called "Kolokol" (The Bell) with Alexander Herzen. In 1863, he joined an uprising in Poland but was unable to join and instead spent time in Switzerland and Italy. In 1868, Bakunin joined the International Working Men's Association, leading a group that quickly gained power within it. The 1872 Hague congress was dominated by arguments between him and Marx. Marx wanted to use the state to bring about socialism, while Bakunin argued for replacing the state with self-governing workplaces and communities. Bakunin could not attend this meeting, so his group lost the debate. He was later expelled from the International for what Marx saw as secret organizations within it. From 1870 until his death in 1876, Bakunin wrote important books like "Statism and Anarchy" and "God and the State." He continued to support worker and peasant movements. In 1870, he participated in an uprising in Lyon, France. His health declining, he attempted a failed insurrection in Italy but had to return to Switzerland. Bakunin is remembered as a key figure in anarchism and opposed Marxism, especially the idea of a dictatorship by the proletariat. He also predicted that Marxist regimes would become one-party dictatorships over workers rather than for them. His book "God and the State" has been widely translated and still influences modern anarchists like Noam Chomsky. Bakunin's influence extended to many thinkers including Peter Kropotkin, Errico Malatesta, and others involved in the anti-globalization movement today.
Zoran Bata Mirkovic, born on September 21, 1971, is a Serbian former football player who is now a coach.

Canillo is a town in Andorra. It's also the main town of a parish there. Canillo is known for its religious importance, with the Sanctuary and Chapel of Our Lady of Meritxell, which celebrates Andorra’s patron saint. The parish has one of the best-preserved Romanesque churches in the Pyrenees called Sant Joan de Caselles. In 2011, Canillo had about 4,826 people living there. Even though it attracts tourists, many residents still raise animals and farm.

Mount Jackson is a town in Shenandoah County, Virginia, United States. The 2010 census showed that it had 1,994 people. For travelers on the highway, Mount Jackson is easy to spot from exit 273 of I-81. You'll see a water tower painted like a basket of apples. Recently, it was repainted. People who explore off the highway can learn about Mount Jackson's history as an important commercial and railroad center in the area. It also has connections to the Civil War and is part of a historic district listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

The Barents Sea is part of the Arctic Ocean, north of Norway and Russia. It is divided between Norwegian and Russian waters. In medieval times, Russians called it the Murmansk Sea or the Norwegian Sea. Today, it's named after Willem Barentsz, a Dutch sailor. This sea is fairly shallow, with an average depth of around 200 meters. It’s important for fishing and looking for oil and gas. The Barents Sea borders the Kola Peninsula to the south, the Norwegian Sea to the west, and islands like Svalbard, Franz Josef Land, and Novaya Zemlya to the north and east. Novaya Zemlya is an extension of the Ural Mountains. It separates the Barents Sea from the Kara Sea. Although part of the Arctic Ocean, the Barents Sea has been called a "hot spot" for warming due to climate change. Changes in weather patterns across Eurasia could result from reduced sea ice and less water mixing in this area.

A migraine is a common type of headache that comes back often. It feels strong to very painful, usually on one side of the head. These headaches can last from hours to three days and feel throbbing or pulsing. Along with pain, people may also feel sick to their stomach, throw up, or be sensitive to light, sound, or smells. Movement makes the pain worse. Before puberty, slightly more boys get migraines than girls, but after that, twice as many women are affected compared to men. The risk of getting migraines often decreases during pregnancy and after menopause. Migraines happen because of a mix of environmental and genetic factors. They usually run in families. Common treatments include simple pain relievers like ibuprofen or acetaminophen for the headache, medications for nausea, and avoiding things that trigger attacks. For some, specific medicines like triptans or ergotamines may help if regular pain relief doesn't work. Adding caffeine might also be useful. To prevent migraines, doctors can prescribe medicines such as metoprolol, valproate, or topiramate. Globally, about 15% of people have migraines, which often start during puberty and are worst in middle age. As of 2016, migraines were one of the leading causes of disability worldwide. An early description similar to migraines is found in the Ebers Papyrus from ancient Egypt around 1500 BC. The word "migraine" comes from Greek meaning 'pain on half the head.'

Gerald Elliot "Jerry" Heller, born on October 6, 1940, and passed away on September 2, 2016, was an American music manager and businessman. He is famous for managing West Coast rap and gangsta rap groups like N.W.A and Eazy-E. In the 1960s and 1970s, he became well-known by bringing Elton John and Pink Floyd to their first big tours in America. He also worked with artists such as Journey, Marvin Gaye, Van Morrison, War, Eric Burdon, Crosby Stills & Nash, Ike & Tina Turner, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Otis Redding, The Who, Reo Speedwagon, Black Sabbath, Humble Pie, Styx, The Grass Roots, and The Standells. In the 1980s, he managed artists like Michel'le, World Class Wreckin' Cru, J.J. Fad, The D.O.C., Egyptian Lover, and La Dream Team. Heller helped West Coast rap music grow when he managed Ruthless Records with Eazy-E and discovered or worked with groups such as N.W.A, The Black Eyed Peas, Above the Law, The D.O.C., and Bone Thugs-N-Harmony. Dr. Dre brought The D.O.C. and Above the Law to Ruthless in its early days, while Eazy introduced Bone later on.

Atal Bihari Vajpayee was born on December 25, 1924, and passed away on August 16, 2018. He was a leader in India who became prime minister three times—first for 13 days in 1996, then for 13 months from 1998 to 1999, and finally for a full term from 1999 to 2004. Vajpayee was part of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and became India's first non-Indian National Congress prime minister to serve a complete term. He also wrote poems and books. Vajpayee spent over five decades in India’s parliament, being elected ten times to the Lok Sabha (the lower house) and twice to the Rajya Sabha (the upper house). He represented Lucknow until he stopped active politics in 2009 due to health issues. Vajpayee was one of the founders of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh (BJS), which became the BJP, with Vajpayee as its first president. During his time as prime minister, India did some important nuclear tests in Pokhran-II in 1998. He tried to befriend Pakistan by visiting Lahore on a bus to meet Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. After a war between India and Pakistan in 1999 over Kargil, Vajpayee worked with President Pervez Musharraf of Pakistan to improve relations. Vajpayee’s birthday, December 25, is now called Good Governance Day in his honor. In 2015, he was given India's highest civilian award, the Bharat Ratna, by President Pranab Mukherjee. Vajpayee died on August 16, 2018, due to old age.

In the 1976 Democratic primaries, voters chose the party's candidate for the U.S. presidency that year. Jimmy Carter, a former governor of Georgia, won this nomination through primary elections and caucuses. The process ended at the 1976 Democratic National Convention in New York City from July 12 to July 15.

Sir Georg Solti, born György Stern on October 21, 1912, and died September 5, 1997, was a Hungarian-born British conductor. He was famous for working with opera companies in Munich, Frankfurt, and London, and as the long-time music director of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. Born in Budapest, Solti studied there under Béla Bartók, Leó Weiner, and Ernestő Dohnányi. In the 1930s, he worked as a répétiteur at the Hungarian State Opera and at the Salzburg Festival for Arturo Toscanini. Due to the rise of Nazi influence in Hungary, Solti left his country in 1938 because of anti-Jewish laws. He conducted a season of Russian ballet at the Royal Opera House in London before fleeing to Switzerland during World War II. There, he earned money as a pianist since he could not conduct. After the war, Solti was appointed music director of the Bavarian State Opera in Munich in 1946. In 1952, he moved to Oper Frankfurt and stayed there for nine years before becoming a citizen of West Germany in 1953. In 1961, Solti became musical director at Covent Garden, London, where his changes improved the company's standards. He was granted the title "The Royal Opera" during his tenure. In 1969, Solti became music director of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra for 22 years. He left this position in 1991 and became its laureate conductor until he died. During his time with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Solti also served as principal conductor of the Orchestre de Paris from 1972 to 1975 and music director of the London Philharmonic Orchestra from 1979 to 1983. Solti was known for his intense performances early in his career. He recorded many works multiple times throughout his life, making over 250 recordings, including 45 complete opera sets. His recording of Wagner's "Der Ring des Nibelungen" is particularly famous and highly regarded. This recording won him two polls as the greatest ever made—once by Gramophone magazine in 1999 and again by BBC Music Magazine in 2012. Throughout his career, Solti received numerous Grammy awards as a recording artist.

Noel George Williams, also called King Sporty, was born on September 19, 1943, and passed away on January 5, 2015. He was a DJ, reggae musician, and record producer for the Tashamba and Konduko labels. King Sporty is famous for writing the song "Buffalo Soldier," which became popular with Bob Marley's version.

In Norse beliefs, Niflheim is an icy place connected to Hel. The name "Niflheim" appears in only two old stories: "Gylfaginning" and "Hrafnagaldr Óðins." It was a world of ice and cold, with frozen rivers like Élivágar and the boiling well Hvergelmir. According to "Gylfaginning," Niflheim came from Ginnungagap, along with Muspelheim, which is the realm of fire. When their elements mixed, they created something that started life on Earth. Later, Niflheim became Hel’s home, where people who didn’t die a heroic or important death went after they died.
Paul Malékou, who was born on November 17, 1938, became the foreign minister of Gabon in 1968. He was born in Fougamou, Gabon. From 1975 to 1983, he worked as the director-general of Asecna.
George Foster Peabody was an American banker and philanthropist from July 27, 1852, to March 4, 1938.
Higdon is a small town in Cleburne County, Arkansas, United States. In 2010, there were 120 people living there.

Francis George Steiner, fba, was born on April 23, 1929, and died on February 3, 2020. He was a literary critic, essayist, philosopher, novelist, and educator from France and the United States. Steiner wrote about language, literature, and their connection to society, as well as how the Holocaust affected them. An article in "The Guardian" called him a "polyglot and polymath." Many people admired Steiner and thought he was one of the greatest minds in today's literary world. A.S. Byatt, an English novelist, described him as a "late renaissance man who explores important ideas of our time." Harriet Harvey-Wood, a former literature director at the British Council, said Steiner was a great lecturer with prophetic insights, often appearing without notes. Steiner taught at several prestigious universities: he was a professor of English and comparative literature at the University of Geneva from 1974 to 1994. From 1994 to 1995, he was a professor of comparative literature and fellow at Oxford University. He also served as a professor of poetry at Harvard University for one year, from 2001 to 2002. Additionally, since 1969, he has been an extraordinary fellow at Churchill College, Cambridge.

Anseba Region is one of Eritrea's six administrative areas, located in the north. Its capital and largest city is Keren. Anseba Region gets its name from the Anseba River, which flows through much of it. The region has an average elevation of about 1,800 meters. It's hottest in May when temperatures can reach up to 32°C, while December to February are the coldest months with freezing temperatures. Anseba Region receives around 467 mm of rainfall annually and is good for farming. In 2005, Anseba had about 549,000 people, which was a growth of 11.80% from 484,200 in 2001. The area covers 23,200 square kilometers with a population density of 23.66 per square kilometer. The People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), formerly the Eritrean Liberation Front, is the ruling authoritarian government. Local and regional elections happen regularly but are limited. Anyone, regardless of ethnicity or religion, can vote. Only PFDJ can participate in elections, which are supervised by its representatives.

Kimberley Gail Marsh, born June 13, 1976, is an English actress and former singer-songwriter. She became famous in 2001 after winning a spot in the band Hear'say by appearing on the TV show "Popstars." Hear'say had some success, with two UK number one hits and an album at number one, but Marsh left the band in 2002 to try singing solo. In 2003, she released an album called "Standing Tall," which reached number nine in the UK charts and had two top ten singles. From April 2006 to December 2019, she played Michelle Connor on the TV show "Coronation Street." She won awards for her acting: Best Newcomer at the 2007 British Soap Awards and National Television Awards, and Best Female Dramatic Performance at the 2017 British Soap Awards. In 2010, she was fourth place in "Popstar to Operastar," a show where famous pop stars learned to sing opera.

Salt Lake County is in Utah, United States. As of 2010 and July 1, 2019, it had about 1 million people, making it Utah's most populous county. Salt Lake City, its largest city and state capital, serves as the county seat. The county was created in 1850. With over 1 million people, it ranks as the 37th most populous county in the U.S., and is one of four mountain counties among the top 100. Salt Lake County includes parts of the Salt Lake Valley and surrounding mountains, like the Oquirrh Mountains to the west and Wasatch Range to the east. The northwestern part has some of Great Salt Lake. It’s known for ski resorts, with Salt Lake City hosting the 2002 Winter Olympics. Salt Lake County is in the center of the Salt Lake City metropolitan area.

La Bollène-Vésubie is a commune in Alpes-Maritimes, which is in the Provence-Alpes-Côte-d’Azur region of southeastern France. The people who live there are called bollénois. In the Niçois dialect of langue d'oc, it's called La Boulèna, and the inhabitants are known as "lu boulenasc."

Toy Purina lived from 1760 to 1799. She was a medicine woman belonging to the Tongva nation, also called the Gabrieliño because they were connected with San Gabriel Mission. Toy Purina opposed Spanish missionaries who ruled California. In 1785, she helped plan an attack on San Gabriel Mission. She recruited six out of eight villages to participate in this rebellion.

Wii Music is a music video game for Nintendo's Wii console. It was released in Japan and North America in October 2008, and in Europe and Australia the next month. This game belongs to both Nintendo’s Touch! Generations brand and the Wii series. In Wii Music, players create music by controlling members of an on-screen band. They can choose from various instruments like guitar or drums and play them using the Wii Remote and Nunchuk. Unlike games like Guitar Hero or Rock Band, there is no scoring for your performance; instead, you are encouraged to try different ways of playing songs. Nintendo advertised this game as a fun way to experience music at home without expensive lessons. It was one of the first announced Wii titles, shown at E3 in 2006 and later in more detail in 2008. Reviews were mixed to positive upon release. Some liked it, but many criticized its simple gameplay, imprecise controls, and use of public-domain music. As a result, it's seen as an unusual game in the Wii series and was not very commercially successful, selling about 2.65 million copies worldwide by March 2009.

Splosion Man is a video game where you play as Splosion Man, who can explode and restart in different places. It's a 2.5D action platform game made by Twisted Pixel Games for Xbox 360, available on Xbox Live Arcade. The game came out on July 22, 2009, during the Xbox Live Summer of Arcade. In the game, you control Splosion Man as he moves through a laboratory called Big Science to escape. Players liked the game and voted it the best original Xbox Live Arcade game in 2009. It was also named one of the top 25 Xbox Live Arcade games by IGN. By the end of 2011, over 487,000 copies had been sold. There's a sequel called Ms. Splosion Man that came out on July 13, 2011.

Hanau is a town in Hesse, Germany, near Frankfurt am Main. It is part of the Frankfurt Rhine-Main area and has a train station that is an important railway junction. The town is also known for its river port on the Main River. Hanau was born in this town, as were brothers Jakob and Wilhelm Grimm, and Franciscus Sylvius. Since the 1500s, Hanau was famous for working with precious metals, especially goldsmithing. Today, it's home to Heraeus, a big family-owned German company. During World War II, much of Hanau was destroyed in an air raid by British forces in 1945. About one-sixth of the population died in the firestorm, and most buildings were damaged or gone. In 1963, Hanau hosted a big festival called Hessentag. Before 2005, it was the main town for Main-Kinzig County. On February 18, 2020, a man attacked two hookah shops in Hanau and killed nine people from outside Germany before killing himself.

Barsha Lekhi (Nepali: बर्शा लेखी) was born on May 5, 1993, in Saptari, Nepal. She is a beauty queen and an environmental activist. In 2016, she won the Miss Nepal title. That same year, she also got the People's Choice Award at Missosology. Barsha represented Nepal at the Miss International contest held in Japan on October 27, 2016. She studied Environmental Science at Patan Multiple Campus. Currently, she is studying for a master’s degree in Environmental Science at Jawaharlal Nehru University. She has also worked with the NEFIN-REDD/CC partnership program.

Robie Creek is a small community in Boise County, Idaho. It had 1,162 people living there as of the 2010 census. The area has a recreation park with swimming, a play area for children, and boat launch. There are no restrooms at the park, but there are portable toilets. Cell phone service is not available there.

Eduardo Horacio Laborde was born on October 19, 1967, and played rugby union. He represented Argentina's national team "Los Pumas" and played three games during the 1991 Rugby World Cup. Eduardo died in February 2015 after a bicycle accident near Pinamar, a coastal town.

Charles Joseph Scarborough, born on April 9, 1963, is an American cable news host. He co-hosts "Morning Joe" with his wife Mika Brzezinski on MSNBC. Previously, he hosted "Scarborough Country" on the same network. Before his career in media, he was a lawyer and served as a politician in the United States House of Representatives from 1995 to 2001 for Florida's 1st district as a Republican. He also worked as a visiting fellow at the Harvard Institute of Politics at the Harvard Kennedy School of Government. In 2011, he was included in "Time" 100, a list of the most influential people in the world.

The Bari province was in Apulia, Italy. Its capital city was Bari. The province had an area and a population of 1,594,109 people (in 2005). On January 1, 2015, the province became the Metropolitan City of Bari.

Edmond Maires (born on January 24, 1931, died on October 1, 2017) was a leader in French labor unions. From 1971 to 1988, he worked as the secretary general of the French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT). He did not like strikes and believed in sharing work more equally.

Annopolis is a place in Crawford County, Illinois, United States. It is located north-northwest of Robinson. Annopolis has a post office with the zip code 62413. As of 2010, its population was 55 people.

Nelson Lagoon (in Unangax̂, called "niilsanam alĝuudaa") is a small place in the Aleutians East Borough of Alaska. In 2010, it had 52 people, down from 83 in 2000. Nelson Lagoon started around 1960 and is one of the newest communities there. It's the only Aleut settlement on the Bering Sea coast. The town sits on a narrow sand spit near the Alaska Peninsula. It’s an important place for fishing, especially salmon. A new dock, boat ramp, office, and storage building were built in the late 1990s. There are good places to park boats and keep gear there. Nelson Lagoon has a runway that is 4,000 feet long, with lights at night, which lets airplanes land regularly. In March 2016, ash fell on Nelson Lagoon during a big eruption of Mount Pavlof nearby.

euro disco is a type of dance music that came from disco in the late 1970s. It mixes pop and rock with a continuous dancing feel. Many euro disco songs have English lyrics, even though singers may speak other languages. Euro disco has two main types: space disco from the late 1970s and italo disco from the early 1980s. By 1986, this music style became less popular, giving way to electronic rock and hi-nrg. However, there was a small revival of italo disco in the late 1990s.

St. Paul is a town in southern Madison County, Arkansas, United States. It had 113 people according to the 2010 census. The town is near the northwest Arkansas region. St. Paul was created in 1887 when the railroad reached that spot.

Milan Michálek was born on December 7, 1984. He plays ice hockey and is a left winger. Currently, he has no team to play for. Recently, he played for the Toronto Maple Leafs in the NHL. In 2003, he was chosen sixth overall by the San Jose Sharks in the NHL draft. His older brother, Zbyněk Michálek, used to be a defenceman and last played in the NHL with the Arizona Coyotes.

Mel Campos López Jr. was born on September 1, 1935, and passed away on January 1, 2017. He was a Filipino politician who became the mayor of Manila from 1986 to 1987 and again from 1988 to 1992. He also served as an assemblyman in the Batasang Pambansa from 1984 to 1986. Additionally, he was the former chairman of the Philippine Sports Commission.

Russian Mission is a city in Alaska, in Kusilvak Census Area. In 1842, it had a fur trading post run by the Russian-American Company. After Russia sold its American possessions to the U.S. in 1867, the city was officially named Russian Mission early in the 1900s. Alcohol cannot be sold there. The population grew from 296 in 2000 to 312 by 2010.

George Dureau lived from December 28, 1930, to April 7, 2014. He was an American artist who worked for many years. His most famous works were charcoal sketches and black and white photographs of poor athletes—both white and black—and dwarfs, as well as amputees. Robert Mapplethorpe said he got inspired by Dureau's photos of amputees and dwarfs. These images showed the people "exposed and vulnerable," but also "playful and needy" and "complex and entirely human."
Domecy-sur-Le-Vaulx is a village in Yonne. It is located in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, which is in central France. Domecy-sur-Le-Vaulx is famous for Château de Domecy-sur-Le-Vaulx.

Sir John Berry Hobbs, known as Jack Hobbs, was an English cricketer who played from 1905 to 1934 for Surrey and for England in 61 test matches between 1908 and 1930. He is called "the master" and seen by experts as one of the best batsmen in cricket history. Hobbs scored 61,760 runs and made 199 centuries in first-class cricket. A right-handed player who also bowled occasionally, Hobbs was very good at fielding, especially at cover point. Born poor in 1882, Hobbs wanted to be a cricketer since he was young. His early batting wasn't great, but he improved suddenly in 1901 and caught the attention of local teams. In 1903, with help from England batsman Tom Hayward, he joined Surrey successfully. Hobbs' reputation grew, and when he could play for Surrey, he did well on his first-class debut. He scored 88 runs in his first match and a century in the next. He became a top county player over the seasons and made his test debut for England in 1908, scoring 83 in his first innings. After some mixed performances for England initially, Hobbs' success against South African spin bowlers helped him stay as an English batsman. In 1911-12, he scored three centuries against Australia and was judged the world's best batsman by critics. In county cricket, Hobbs played with an attacking style until 1914. During World War I in the Royal Flying Corps, Hobbs kept his reputation when cricket resumed in 1919. Appendicitis threatened his career but he returned as a more cautious player in 1921 and scored well in both test and domestic cricket before retiring. Hobbs played some of his best innings during this period. His success came from fast footwork, ability to play many shots, and good placement. He was one of the first batsmen to succeed against spin bowlers and adapted his technique early in his career. Hobbs was very successful on difficult batting grounds as an opener, forming partnerships with Tom Hayward, Andy Sandham for Surrey, and Wilfred Rhodes, Herbert Sutcliffe for England. Hobbs' partnership with Sutcliffe is still the best for the first wicket in test history. People thought highly of Hobbs back then, and critics continue to rank him among the best batsmen ever. Hobbs lived comfortably with his wife Ada after retiring, using his wages from Surrey, commercial deals, and income from a sporting goods shop he opened in 1921. After cricket, he worked as a journalist. Knighted in 1953, he spent his later years taking care of Ada until both died just months apart in 1963 at the ages of 81.

william john fairbairn, born on January 7, 1947, is a former professional ice hockey player. He was known as "Bulldog" Fairbairn and played as a right wing. Fairbairn played in the NHL for 10 seasons. Most of his career was with the New York Rangers. Later, he also played for the Minnesota North Stars and St. Louis Blues. He retired early in the 1978-79 NHL season. During his career, he scored 162 goals.

The Central Bohemian region is a part of the Czech Republic. It is in the middle of what used to be called Bohemia. Prague, which is the capital city of the Czech Republic, is the main city here but it is not part of this region. Instead, it has its own area. This region is big - 11,014 square kilometers, almost 14% of all land in the Czech Republic. It surrounds Prague and touches other regions like Liberec to the north, Hradec Králové to the northeast, Pardubice to the east, Vysočina to the southeast, South Bohemia to the south, Plzeň to the west, and Ústí nad Labem to the northwest.

The Berlin State Opera is on Unter den Linden Boulevard in the historic center of Berlin. It was built from 1741 to 1743, ordered by Frederick the Great and designed by Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff in Palladian style. The opera house was damaged during World War II bombing. Afterward, it was rebuilt from 1951 to 1955 as part of Forum Fridericianum square. It's known as "Lindenoper" and is the first theater in any city to stand alone as a prominent, large building.

Kieren John Perkins, OAM, was born on August 14, 1973. He is an Australian swimmer who used to compete. Perkins won four Olympic medals and held world records in three events. Known as one of the best long-distance swimmers globally, he achieved two gold medals in the 1500-meter freestyle at the 1992 and 1996 Olympics, plus a silver medal in 2000.

Fernando Bernabé Agüero Rocha was born on June 11, 1917, in Managua and died on September 27, 2011. He was a Nicaraguan politician and the founder of the Social Conservative Party in 1988. In 1967, Agüero represented the conservative National Opposition Union (UNO) in the presidential election against the Somoza regime. His campaign had violent incidents, including the bloody repression of one of his rallies in Managua. Four years later, in 1971, Agüero signed a controversial pact called Kupia Kumi with Anastasio Somoza Debayle.

Joel Murray, born on April 17, 1963, is an American actor. He was in famous TV shows like "Mad Men," "Grand," "Love & War," "Dharma & Greg," and "Shameless." He also acted in movies such as "God Bless America" and "Monsters University."

The Legend of Zelda: Spirit Tracks is a game for Nintendo DS. It's part of the Legend of Zelda series and came out in December 2009. In this game, you can play as Link, who uses a steam train to travel across the land. You can also control phantoms and play the spirit flute. The game was later released on Wii U in October 2016. Spirit Tracks is special because it has different endings based on your actions.

The Ringmaster is a music album from the American hip hop group Insane Clown Posse. It was released on March 8, 1994, through Psychopathic Records. Recording took place in 1993 at the Tempermill studio. This album is part of their "Dark Carnival" story. The songs talk about a carnival leader who acts like a judge deciding what happens to people after they die. This leader is made from the listener's bad actions. The Ringmaster was mainly created by producer Mike E. Clark and he worked with the group for many years. It includes appearances by other artists, Capitol E and Jumpsteady. In 1998, Island Records released the album again. The RIAA later awarded it a gold certification. In 2004, the original version also received a gold certification.

Hammurabi, the sixth king of Babylonia from around 1792 BC to 1750 BC (middle chronology), succeeded his father Sin-muballit due to his father's poor health. During Hammurabi’s reign, he conquered Elam and several city-states like Larsa, Eshnumna, and Mari. He forced the King of Assyria, Ishme-dagan I, and his son Mut-ashkur, to pay tribute. As a result, almost all of Mesopotamia came under Babylonian control. Hammurabi is famous for creating the Code of Hammurabi, which he said was given by Shamash, the god of justice. Unlike earlier codes like Ur-Nammu’s, his code focused more on punishing the person who committed the crime rather than just compensating the victim. It outlined specific punishments for each crime and was among the first to assume innocence until proven guilty. While its punishments are very strict today, they were meant to limit revenge by a wronged person. The Code of Hammurabi and the Law of Moses in the Torah share many similarities. Hammurabi was considered divine during his lifetime. After his death, he was remembered as a great conqueror who spread civilization and made everyone honor Marduk, the god of Babylon. His military achievements were later downplayed, but his role as an ideal lawgiver became central to his legacy. For Mesopotamians, Hammurabi’s reign set the standard for past events. Even after his empire fell, he was still seen as a good ruler, and many kings in the region considered him their ancestor. Hammurabi was found by archaeologists in the late 1800s and is now recognized as an important figure in the history of law.

Townsville is a city on the north-eastern coast of Queensland, Australia. It's the largest city in that part of Queensland, with about 180,820 people living there as of June 2018. Locals call it the unofficial capital of North Queensland because it has many important government offices and businesses. The city is near the Great Barrier Reef. Townsville is also a big industrial place with one of the world's largest zinc refineries and other similar factories. Its port is being expanded to handle bigger ships from Asia and around the world. Popular places to visit include "The Strand," a long beach with gardens, Riverway, a park by Ross River, Reef HQ Aquarium with many sea animals, and the Museum of Tropical Queensland. There’s also Castle Hill, an important landmark for exercise, the Townsville Sports Reserve, and Magnetic Island, which is mostly a national park.

A resistance movement is an organized effort by some people in a country to oppose the government or an occupying power, aiming to cause disruption. It can use nonviolent methods, like protests, or force, which may include weapons. Sometimes, different groups within a country might use both violent and non-violent tactics. The idea of whether armed resistance is legal has been debated since 1899 when international treaties were first made about the laws of war. In 1899, a rule called the Martens Clause was added to address disagreements over francs-tireurs—fighters who weren't part of a regular army. More recently, in 1977, an agreement related to protecting victims in wars said that people fighting against colonial control or racist regimes could be considered legitimate. However, this isn’t always clear and can lead to different views. Depending on how a government sees it, a resistance group might be seen as a terrorist organization if its members are not recognized as lawful fighters who have the right to resist occupation. This decision is often based on political judgment.
Guerbigny is a village in Somme, which is in Hauts-de-France, a region in northern France.

Stagecoach is a transportation company based in Perth, Scotland. It runs buses, express coaches, and trams in the United Kingdom. The company used to operate in Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, and Oceania. Its shares are listed on the London Stock Exchange.

squash is a racket and ball game. Two players hit a small, hollow rubber ball against the four walls of a court with their racquets. They take turns hitting the ball onto any playable surface of the court. The aim is to make it difficult for the opponent to return the ball properly. About 20 million people regularly play squash in more than 185 countries. There is a governing body called the World Squash Federation (WSF). It is recognized by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), but squash is not included in the Olympics. Many people support adding it to future Olympic programs.

Sidney Sheldon, born on February 11, 1917, and passed away on January 30, 2007, was an American writer. He also worked as a director and producer. In the 1930s, he began his career by writing plays for Broadway. Later, he moved to movies where he wrote successful scripts. One of his famous works, "The Bachelor and the Bobby-Soxer" (1947), won him an Oscar in 1948. He then worked in television from the 1960s to the early 1980s. Some popular shows he created include "The Patty Duke Show" (1963-1966), "I Dream of Jeannie" (1965-1970), and "Hart to Hart" (1979-1984). After turning 50, Sheldon started writing best-selling romantic suspense novels like "Master of the Game" (1982), "The Other Side of Midnight" (1973), and "Rage of Angels" (1980). His 18 novels were read by millions—over 300 million copies sold in more than 50 languages. He is often mentioned among the top ten best-selling fiction writers ever.

Those merging with other rivers are ordered from closest to farthest from the sea. Some non-German rivers, like the Meuse, are noted for their German tributaries and appear in italics. The University of Costa Rica (Spanish: "Universidad de Costa Rica", abbreviated UCR) is a public university in Costa Rica. Its main campus, Ciudad Universitaria Rodrigo Facio, is in San Pedro Montes de Oca, part of the San José province. Founded in 1843 as "Universidad de Santo Tomás," it's the oldest and largest higher education institution in Costa Rica. UCR is a leading research university in both Costa Rica and Central America, known for being one of the most prestigious and recognized in Latin America. Around 45,000 students study there each year.

James Henry Hammond, born on November 15, 1807, and died on November 13, 1864, was a lawyer, politician, and plantation owner from South Carolina. He was a U.S. representative from 1835 to 1836. Later, he served as the 60th governor of South Carolina from 1842 to 1844, and then as a U.S. senator from 1857 to 1860. He was known for speaking strongly in favor of slavery before the American Civil War. Through his marriage, Hammond owned large areas of land, several plantations, houses, and more than 300 slaves. He was also related to Wade Hampton II through his wife's family. His sister-in-law's children included Wade Hampton III. Hammond faced a scandal when he was found out for raping four teenage nieces from the Hampton family. Initially, this seemed to hurt his political career, but later he was still elected as a U.S. senator.

Shawnee is a city in Pottawatomie County, Oklahoma, United States. The population was 29,857 in 2010. This number increased by 4.9 percent from 28,692 in 2000. The city is part of the Oklahoma City-Shawnee combined statistical area. It is also the county seat of Pottawatomie County and the main city of the Shawnee micropolitan statistical area. Shawnee is close to Interstate 40. It's about a 45-minute drive east of downtown Oklahoma City. To the east and northeast, it is 112 miles from the McClellan-Kerr Arkansas River Navigation System. This system offers barge access to the Gulf of Mexico.

The Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) was a self-governing area in the Philippines, mainly covering five provinces with large Muslim populations: Basilan (excluding Isabela City), Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao, Sulu, and Tawi-Tawi. This region had its own government. Cotabato City served as the main seat of this government, though it was not part of ARMM's area. From 2006 to July 16, 2008, ARMM also included Shariff Kabunsuan province. However, the Supreme Court declared the law creating this province unconstitutional, and Shariff Kabunsuan ceased to exist as a province. In October 2012, President Benigno Aquino III aimed for peace in the region and proposed renaming it the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region. On July 26, 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte signed the Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL), leading to the formation of the new Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The ARMM officially ended after BOL's ratification on January 25, 2019. The BARMM will take its place with the help of a transitional government called the Bangsamoro Transition Authority.

The current flag of Myanmar, also called Burma, was adopted on October 21, 2010. This replaced the older flag used since 1974. The new flag came with changes to the country's name, which were written in the 2008 constitution. The flag has three horizontal stripes: yellow, green, and red. In the middle is a white star with five points. The yellow stripe means solidarity, the green one peace and tranquility, and the red one courage and decisiveness.
Awista Ayub, born around 1979, is an Afghan writer. She also founded the Afghan Youth Sports Exchange in the United States.

Orestes "Minnie" Miñoso, born Saturnino Orestes Armas Miñoso Arrieta (November 29, 1925 – March 1, 2015), was a Cuban professional baseball player. He played in the negro leagues starting in 1946 and became an all-star third baseman for the New York Cubans. After baseball's color line broke down in 1948, Miñoso joined the Cleveland Indians of Major League Baseball (MLB) and later the Chicago White Sox. As a black Cuban player, he was one of the first to play in MLB and the first for the White Sox. Miñoso played as an all-star left fielder for seven seasons with the Indians and White Sox. He won gold gloves for three seasons when he was older. Miñoso batted well for eight seasons. He led the league in triples and stolen bases three times each, and in hits, doubles, and total bases once each. Miñoso and Willie Mays were credited for bringing speed back as a way to score runs in the 1950s. Miñoso was known for getting on base; he led the American League (AL) in being hit by a pitch ten times and held that record from 1959 to 1985. Miñoso was an excellent defender, leading AL left fielders in assists six times and in putouts and double plays four times each. He was very popular and played for the White Sox, helping them become one of the best teams during the 1950s and 1960s. Miñoso also held the White Sox record for home runs from 1956 to 1974. After leaving MLB in 1964, Miñoso played and managed in Mexico until 1973. He later coached for the White Sox and made brief appearances as a player in 1976 and 1980. In 1983, his number 9 was retired by the White Sox, and a statue of him was unveiled at U.S. Cellular Field in 2004. Miñoso was honored in Cuba's baseball hall of fame in exile in 1983 and Mexico's professional baseball hall of fame in 1996. In 2014, he was considered for the National Baseball Hall of Fame, but didn't make it that year.

The River Shannon is Ireland's longest river. It drains a basin covering one-fifth of Ireland's land area. The Shannon divides western Ireland (mainly Connacht) from eastern and southern parts (Leinster and most of Munster). County Clare, though west of the river, belongs to Munster. There are fewer than thirty-five places to cross between Limerick in the south and Dowra in the north. The river is named after a Celtic goddess called Sionna. The Shannon has been important since ancient times; it was first mapped by Ptolemy, a Greek-Egyptian geographer. The river flows mostly south from a source near Cavan before turning west into the Atlantic Ocean through a long estuary. Limerick city is where freshwater meets saltwater in the estuary. The Shannon is tidal up to the base of the Ardnacrusha dam east of Limerick.

The Fahrenheit scale is based on a system proposed by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, who lived from 1686 to 1736. It uses degrees Fahrenheit (°F) as its unit. There are different stories about how he set the initial points of this scale. One account suggests that 0 °F was meant to be the freezing point of a mixture of ice, water, and ammonium chloride. He also set another point at his estimate for the average human body temperature, which was around 96 °F (about 2.6 °F lower than today’s value). He marked a middle point at 32 °F, equivalent to the freezing temperature of pure water. Today, the Fahrenheit scale is defined by two fixed points: the freezing point of water is set at 32 °F, and the boiling point of water is 212 °F (at sea level under standard atmospheric pressure). This scale was the first standardized one widely used. However, it’s not commonly used in most countries now. In the United States and some of its territories, as well as a few other places like Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, the Cayman Islands, and Liberia, Fahrenheit is still the official temperature scale. Some islands that use the same weather service, such as Antigua and Barbuda, St. Kitts and Nevis, The Bahamas, and Belize, also use it alongside Celsius. A few British overseas territories like the U.S. Virgin Islands, Montserrat, Anguilla, and Bermuda still use both scales. In the United Kingdom, temperatures are often given in both Fahrenheit and Celsius because some people prefer Fahrenheit or for stylistic reasons. Most countries now officially use the Celsius scale, which was renamed from centigrade in 1948 to honor Anders Celsius, a Swedish astronomer.

Knott's Berry Farm is a theme park in Bueno Park, California. Cedar Fair owns and runs it. In 2018, it was one of the top 20 most visited parks in North America, with about 4 million visitors yearly. The park has around 40 rides such as roller coasters, family rides, dark rides, and water rides. It started in the 1920s as a roadside berry stand. Walter Knott ran it on State Route 39. By the 1940s, there was also a restaurant, shops, and other fun things like a pretend ghost town for visitors to enjoy. Over the next few decades, the site became more like a modern amusement park. They began charging people money to enter in 1968. In 1997, Cedar Fair bought the park for $300 million. Two years earlier, Knott's food business had been bought by Conagra, Inc. in 1995.
Sorel Etrog was an artist, writer, and philosopher born in Romania and later lived in Israel and Canada. He is famous for his sculptures. He made modern artworks and contemporary sculptures.

Naughton is a village located in Suffolk, England. It's near Ipswich to the north-west and Stowmarket to the south-west. Naughton used to be its own civil parish but merged with Nedging in 1935. In 1931, it had 98 people living there. Naughton is at the meeting point of two roads. One road comes from the southwest and goes to Nedging Tye. The other comes from the southeast. At this junction stands St. Mary's Church, a 14th-century flint-built church in the center of the village, just west of where these roads meet.

Washburn County, in Maine, United States, had 32,856 people according to the 2010 count. It is one of Maine's least populous counties. The main town is Machias. Washburn County was set up on June 25, 1789. It shares a border with New Brunswick in Canada. Some call it "Sunrise County" because it has the easternmost point in the U.S., though others say the sun rises first here for the 48 states together. Many small seaside towns there depend on fishing. Tourism is also important by the shore, but not as much as in other parts of Maine. Blueberries are a big part of the local economy.

The Camp David Accords were two political agreements signed on September 17, 1978. They were signed after 12 days of secret talks at Camp David, which is a place where the U.S. president stays in Maryland. Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin signed these accords at the White House with U.S. President Jimmy Carter as a witness. The second agreement (called "A Framework for the Conclusion of a Peace Treaty Between Egypt and Israel") led directly to the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty. Because of this agreement, Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize. Richard Lester, also called Dick Lester, was born on January 19, 1932. He is a former American film director who now lives in the UK. People know him for directing films with The Beatles in the 1960s and for his work on Superman movies in the 1980s. Lester also has a special connection with London Film School as an honorary associate.

The Detroit Pistons are a basketball team based in Detroit, USA. They play in the National Basketball Association (NBA) and are part of the Eastern Conference's Central Division. Their home games are at Little Caesars Arena in Midtown. The Pistons started as the Fort Wayne (Zollner) Pistons in 1941 in Indiana. They won two championships in 1944 and 1945 when they were in the National Basketball League (NBL). In 1948, they joined the Basketball Association of America (BAA). In 1949, the NBL and BAA combined to form the NBA. The Pistons became part of this new league. In 1957, the team moved to Detroit. Since then, the Pistons have won three NBA championships: in 1989, 1990, and 2004.

Snakes are long, legless reptiles that eat meat. Like other lizard-like animals called squamates, they are cold-blooded and have scales covering their bodies. Some snake species have more flexible jaws, allowing them to eat prey larger than their heads. Their organs, like kidneys, are stacked rather than side-by-side. Most snakes have only one usable lung. Many lizards have evolved into legless forms independently several times, leading to various types of legless lizards that sometimes have eyelids and ears unlike snakes. Snakes live on most continents except Antarctica, including many small islands, with some exceptions like Ireland or Iceland. Some species can grow very long, while others are quite short. Snakes are believed to have come from burrowing or water-living lizards, possibly during the Jurassic period. The earliest snake fossils date back about 143 to 167 million years ago. Most modern snake species appeared after a major extinction event around 66 million years ago. Ancient descriptions of snakes can be found in old writings like the Brooklyn papyrus. Most snakes are not venomous and use their mouths for eating prey, though some have strong enough venom to harm or kill humans. Nonvenomous snakes often squeeze their prey to kill it instead.
Lantsch/Lenz is a village in the Albula area of Graubünden, Switzerland. Most people there speak Romansh.

The team captain in soccer is a chosen player who leads on the field. They are often older or more experienced players, influential in games, or have strong leadership skills. The captain is typically identified by wearing a special arm band.
Bettlach is a small town in Haut-Rhin and Grand Est, which are in northeastern France.

Massimo Mattioli, born on September 25, 1943, and died on August 23, 2019, was an Italian artist who also did cartoons. He started his work in 1965 with a comic book called "Il Vittorioso." In the early 1970s, he moved to London to draw comics for "Mayfair" magazine. Later, he created a character named Pasquino for "Paese Sera" newspaper in 1973. Mattioli also worked on "Il Giornalino," creating another character called Pinky in the same year. In 1977, with Stefano Tamburini, he made an underground magazine called "Cannibale." The first adventure of Joe Galaxy was published in this magazine that year. Mattioli also created a comic series about Squeak the Mouse in 1982; it was a funny story based on Tom and Jerry. He won several prizes, such as the French Phoenix Prize in 1971, and the Golden Romics award in 2009.
Kensington is a town in Montgomery County, Maryland, United States. The 2010 census counted 2,213 people there. Greater Kensington includes the whole 20895 zip code and has about 19,054 people.

Fratton Park is an English football stadium in Portsmouth, a city on the island of Portsea in the UK. It belongs to Portsmouth F.C., which was founded on April 5, 1898. The unique thing about this stadium is that it’s on an island, unlike other professional stadiums in England, because it's built on Portsea Island where Portsmouth is located. It was constructed in 1899 on a potato field in Milton, a village that later became part of Portsmouth as the city grew during the 20th century. Fratton Park opened to the public on August 15, 1899. The first match there was held on September 6, 1899, when Portsmouth beat Southampton F.C. by 2-0; about 4,141 people watched. The stadium’s name comes from Fratton railway station, which is one mile west of Milton in the neighboring Fratton area. They chose this name to make fans think that the stadium was close enough for easy walking or using public transport, even though Milton had no railway station itself. In 1935, Fratton Park could hold up to 58,000 people after rebuilding parts of it, but it never reached that many. The highest number of spectators was 51,385 on February 26, 1949, during a match against Derby County. Since 1996, the stadium has been all-seated, reducing its capacity. Portsmouth fans call their home ground "the old girl," and it’s known as "Fortress Fratton" because of its strong atmosphere. The stadium is part of St. James' Parish in Milton, Portsmouth.

The grand tour was a custom from the 17th and 18th centuries where wealthy young European men, usually British noblemen or those from Protestant northern Europe, traveled through Europe after they grew up, typically around 21 years old. They often had family members with them as chaperones. This trip was seen as an important part of learning about culture and society. The grand tour became popular in the mid-1600s until the 1840s when trains started making travel easier. It usually included visits to famous places like Rome, where young men learned about ancient art and culture. This journey lasted several months to a few years and was guided by knowledgeable tutors or guides. The grand tour continued in popularity even after it lost some of its prestige due to changes in cultural interests. Thomas Cook’s organized tours later made such trips more common for many people. The value of the grand tour lay in experiencing classical art, meeting polite society, and seeing important artworks. In essence, the grand tour was a special kind of trip that wealthy young men took to learn about history and culture before joining adult life. It started as an aristocratic tradition but influenced modern travel ideas and tourist destinations.

The banker horse is a type of feral horse living in North Carolina's Outer Banks. These horses are small, tough, and easy to handle. These horses come from domesticated Spanish horses brought to the Americas in the 16th century. Some might have become wild after surviving shipwrecks or being left on the islands by explorers like Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón or Sir Richard Grenville. Banker horses can be found on Ocracoke Island, Shackleford Banks, Currituck Banks, Cedar Island, and in the Rachel Carson Estuarine Sanctuary. Even though they can step on plants and hurt ground-nesting animals, people let them stay because of their history. They eat marsh grasses that give them water and food, with some help from temporary freshwater pools. To stop overpopulating and inbreeding, and protect their habitat, the horses are managed by the National Park Service, the state of North Carolina, and several private groups. They check for diseases like equine infectious anemia; a 1996 outbreak on Shackleford was found and stopped. These horses are also protected from cars on North Carolina Highway 12. The number of horses is controlled by adopting some out and using birth control. Banker horses that have been trained can be used for trail riding, driving, or occasionally patrolling on horseback.

Miriam Margolyes, born on May 18, 1941, is a character actress and comedian from Britain and Australia. Her first roles were on stage. She then played supporting parts in films and television shows. In 1993, she won a BAFTA award for her role in "The Age of Innocence," directed by Martin Scorsese. Margolyes also acted as Professor Sprout in the Harry Potter movie series. Margolyes has lived in England, Australia, and Italy for many years. She has performed in plays in both countries, including the Australian premiere of a 2013 play. In 2013, she became an Australian citizen.

A chemical substance is a form of matter with a fixed composition and unique properties. It cannot be separated into its components without breaking chemical bonds. Chemical substances can be simple elements, compounds, or alloys. Sometimes, pure chemical elements are also included as chemical substances. These pure substances are often called 'pure' to distinguish them from mixtures. For example, water is always composed of the same ratio of hydrogen and oxygen atoms, whether it comes from a river or a lab. Other common examples include diamond (carbon), gold, table salt (sodium chloride), and sugar (sucrose). In reality, no substance is completely pure, so purity levels are determined by their intended use. Chemical substances can be solids, liquids, gases, or plasma, changing forms with temperature or pressure. Substances can also change form through chemical reactions. Energy forms like light and heat are not considered matter and thus not 'substances' in this context.
multiple-camera production involves using several cameras to record or broadcast a scene at the same time. This method contrasts with a single-camera setup that uses only one camera.

Lopp Lagoon is a tidal lake located near Cape Prince of Wales, at the westernmost tip of the Seward Peninsula, in Alaska. Many small rivers feed into it, but most of the water comes from the Mint River. Some saltwater from the Pacific Ocean enters through channels between the lagoon and the Bering Strait. The lake was named after William Thomas Lopp, a missionary who worked with Inuit people and led an overland relief expedition in 1897-98. Historically, Lopp Lagoon has been important for food sources like salmon and waterfowl for people living in the Wales area of Alaska.
Clay County is in Indiana, a state in the U.S. In 2010, it had 26, 890 people. The main town is called Brazil. Clay County is part of the Terre Haute, Indiana, area.

Rolf Leeser, born in Essen on June 4, 1929, played football for Ajax in the Netherlands from 1948 to 1954. He was Jewish and joined Ajax's youth academy at 12 years old. His first professional game with Ajax happened on September 19, 1948. During the 1951-52 season, Leeser became a regular player. He continued playing until April 1954, scoring six goals in 34 matches for Ajax. Leeser had other jobs too. He designed fashion and created Leeser b.v., a women's clothing company. He also helped redesign the Ajax logo, which is still used today. Rolf Leeser passed away on March 21, 2018, at age 88. He was married to Anita B. Leeser-Gassan.
Trévoux is a small town in the Ain area, which is in eastern France. The people who live there are called Trévoltiens. It is near Lyon and sits on the hillside next to the Saône River.

Maurice Petty was born on March 27, 1939, and passed away on July 25, 2020. He was from the United States. Maurice worked as a crew chief and an engine builder for Petty Enterprises, where he also owned a part. In 2011, he was inducted into the International Motorsports Hall of Fame. Later, in 2014, he became a member of the NASCAR Hall of Fame. He was the first engine builder to be honored this way.

Saint-Julien-de-Mailloc was once its own village in Calvados, a part of Normandy in Northwestern France. It no longer exists as a separate community. On January 1, 2016, it became part of a new village called Vorbiquet.

West Palm Beach is a city and county seat in Florida, United States. It's right next to Palm Beach, which sits on an island across Lake Worth Lagoon. The population was 99,919 in 2010. West Palm Beach is part of the Miami metropolitan area. In 2017, this area had about 6,158,824 people. It's older than Miami, having been a city since November 1894. West Palm Beach is roughly north of downtown Miami.

Those that didn't offer scholarships became division iii. In computer architecture, 64-bit refers to data units that are 64 bits wide. This includes integers and memory addresses in 64-bit CPUs and ALUs. These processors have registers, address buses, or data buses of that size. 64-bit microcomputers use these types of processors. From a software perspective, 64-bit computing means using code with 64-bit virtual memory addresses. However, not all 64-bit instruction sets support full 64-bit virtual memory; for example, x86-64 and ARMv8 only support 48 bits. A 64-bit register can hold over 18 quintillion different values. The range of integer values in 64 bits depends on how the data is represented. In an unsigned binary number, it ranges from 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615. With two's complement representation, it ranges from -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. This means a processor with 64-bit memory addresses can access up to 16 exabytes of memory. A 64-bit computer architecture usually has 64-bit wide registers for data types and addresses. However, the external buses might be different sizes—sometimes larger than the registers. The term "64-bit" also describes processors with 64-bit floating-point numbers.

Tim Francis, born on May 1, 1928, and known as Harold Huyton Francis, was a diplomat from New Zealand. He served as the permanent representative of New Zealand at the United Nations from 1978 to 1982. From 1984 to 1988, he managed Tokelau. Between 1988 and 1991, he was the ambassador to the United States.

györgy sándor ligeti was a composer who created contemporary classical music. He is known as one of the most important avant-garde composers of the late 20th century and one of the most innovative in his time. Born in Transylvania, Romania, Ligeti lived in Hungary for some years before moving to Austria in 1956 due to political reasons. In 1968, he became an Austrian citizen. He taught music at the Hamburg Hochschule für Musik und Theater from 1973 until his retirement in 1989. Ligeti faced restrictions on his musical style under communist Hungary but could fully explore avant-garde music after moving to the West. In Cologne, he experimented with electronic music and later developed a technique called micropolyphony for orchestral works like "Atmosphères". His work "Le Grand Macabre" led him away from chromaticism towards polyrhythm in his later compositions. Ligeti is famous for his music being used in film soundtracks, even though he didn't compose any film scores himself. Some of his pieces were adapted and included in Stanley Kubrick's films, including "2001: A Space Odyssey".

Raise Your Glass" is a song by American singer Pink from her first greatest hits album "Greatest Hits... So Far!!" (2010). The song was written by Pink, Max Martin, and Karl Schuster. It was produced by Max Martin and Karl Schuster, who have made many of Pink's popular songs. The song celebrates the first decade since Pink started singing in 2000. It is dedicated to her fans who have supported her over the years. "Raise Your Glass" came out as the main single from the album on October 5, 2010, through Jive Records. The song was both well-liked by critics and successful commercially. Most music critics praised it as a party song. It reached the top ten in several countries, including the United States, where it became Pink's third number-one single. In 2011, "Raise Your Glass" ranked number thirteen on Jive Records' top 40 year-end chart. The song was used in an advertisement for the 2011 movie "Bridesmaids," and also appeared in trailers for the films "What's Your Number?" and "New Year's Eve.

The Panhard VBL is a French wheel-driven, all-terrain 4x4 vehicle. It's also known as VBL or Panhard. The vehicle comes in different versions. Its design combines the mobility of the Peugeot P4 liaison car with protection against small arms fire, artillery fragments, mines, and NBC weapons. Made between 1985 and 2010, it has been used by French and other European, African, and Central American armies since the 1980s in various conflicts.

Neurosis involves ongoing feelings of distress but does not include delusions or hallucinations. The term is not used by U.S. psychiatrists anymore, as it was removed from the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders" (DSM) in 1980 with the release of DSM-III. Neurosis is different from psychosis, which means losing touch with reality. It is also distinct from neuroticism, a key part of personality often discussed in five-factor models of personality.

Humayun Ahmed was born on November 13, 1948, and passed away on July 19, 2012. He was a Bangladeshi writer who wrote novels, plays, screenplays, made films, wrote songs, and taught as a lecturer. His first big novel, "Nondito Noroke," came out in 1972. Ahmed wrote more than 200 books, both fiction and non-fiction, which were popular in Bangladesh. Many of his books sold the most at the Ekushey Book Fair from the 1990s to 2000s. He won important awards like the Bangla Academy Literary Award in 1981 and the Ekushey Padak in 1994 for his work on Bengali literature. In the early 1990s, Ahmed started making films based on his own novels. He directed a total of eight films and won six Bangladesh National Film Awards for "Daruchini Dip," "Aguner Poroshmoni," and "Ghetuputra Komola." He also had his own film production company called Nuhash Chalachitra.
Ahú Presidio was a prison in Curitiba, Brazil. It opened in 1905 and was the first prison in the city. The prison closed in 2006. Now, the site is used for filming movies and TV shows.
Randall Paul Stout was an architect who worked in Los Angeles, California. He was born on May 6, 1958, and died on July 11, 2014.

Respiratory diseases affect organs and tissues that help animals breathe. They include problems in the airways like the trachea, bronchi, and alveoli, as well as issues with the lungs, pleura, nerves, and muscles involved in breathing. These diseases can be mild, such as a common cold or flu, or very serious, like pneumonia, tuberculosis, or lung cancer. Doctors who study these problems are called pulmonologists. They focus on conditions of the chest and respiratory system. Respiratory diseases can be grouped in several ways: By which part of the breathing system is affected By the signs and symptoms shown Or by what causes the disease

Hispar Pass (also called Hispar La) is a high mountain pass (elevation 5,128 meters or 16,824 feet) in Pakistan's Karakoram Range. At the pass, the Biafo Glacier and Hispar Glacier meet to form the world's longest non-polar glacial traverse, measuring 100 kilometers in length.

Brighton is a village mainly in Macoupin County, Illinois, and partly in Jersey County. In 2010, it had about 2,254 people living there. The mayor now is Michael Roberts. Brighton is part of the Metro-East area and the St. Louis region.
